Now he that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast. And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him. Eagle 🦅 or Duck 🦆?

While waiting in line for a taxi at the airport, I immediately noticed that the taxi that had just pulled up was polished to a mirror shine. The taxi driver, well dressed in a white shirt, black tie and pressed black pants, got out of the car and opened the back door for me. He handed me a laminated card and said, "I'm Wasu, your driver. While I load your luggage into the trunk, I would like you to read my mission statement."
Surprised, I read the card which said:
Wasu's Mission Statement:
To get my customers to their destinations as quickly, safely and economically as possible in a friendly environment.
I was amazed, especially when I noticed that the inside of the taxi was as clean as the outside. Wasu sat behind the wheel and asked, "Would you like a cup of coffee? I have a thermos of regular coffee and a thermos of decaf."
"I jokingly said, "No, I'd prefer a soft drink."
Wasu smiled and replied, "No problem. I have a refrigerator in front with regular and diet Coke, lassi, water, and orange juice." 
Almost stammering, I said, "I'll have a lassi, since I've never had one before." 
As he handed me the drink, Wasu said, "If you want something to read, I have Good Housekeeping magazine, Reader's Digest, the Bible, and Travel + Leisure." 
As we walked away, Wasu handed me another laminated card and said, "These are the stations I get and the music they play, if you want to listen to the radio." 
And to make matters worse, Wasu informed me that he had turned on the heat and asked me if the temperature was comfortable for me. He then advised me on the best route to my destination for that time of day. He also let me know that he would be happy to chat and tell me about the sights we were going to see, or, if I preferred, to leave me with my thoughts. 
"Tell me, Wasu," I asked in amazement, "have you always served customers in this way?"
Wasu smiled in the rearview mirror. "No, not always. In fact, it's only been the last two years. My first five years of driving were spent complaining like all the other taxi drivers. Then one day I heard about the power of choice."
"The power of choice is that you can be a duck or an eagle."
"If you wake up in the morning expecting to have a bad day, you will rarely be disappointed. Stop complaining!"
"Don't be a duck. Be an eagle. Ducks quack and complain. Eagles soar above the crowd."
"That struck me," Wasu said. "He went on to say, 'It's about me. I was always complaining, so I decided to change my ways and become an eagle. I looked at other taxis and their drivers. The taxis were dirty, the drivers were rude, and the customers were unhappy. So I decided to make some changes. I started with a few at a time. When my customers responded well, I made more.'"
"I guess that paid off for you," I said.
"Yes, it definitely did," Wasu replied. "My first year as an eagle, I doubled my income from the year before. This year I'll probably quadruple it. My customers call me on my cell phone for appointments or leave me a message."
Wasu made a different choice. He decided to stop quacking like ducks and start flying like eagles.
Live like an eagle ahead...
—Adapted

Every human has been imprinted in their early life with a pattern I call "the unconscious love blueprint".

In the malleable age from birth through childhood our little sponge brains are absorbing everything, filing it deep inside in our unconscious and subconscious as a learned understanding of how the world works. 

How love works.

This understanding forms a deep part of who we are, whether we are aware of it or not.

It filters through into the narratives we tell about ourselves, and others.

It shapes what we believe love to be, and what it is like to experience it.

Oh, our conscious mind gets patterned in entirely different ways… with grand media-conditioned ideas of grandiose love-stories for the ages.

We will tell ourselves we want those things, we strive for those things, we deserve those things, it’s how love should be!

But… the architecture and structure of the love we actually end up seeking, creating, finding and playing out often takes quite a wide divergence from those fanciful romantic daydreams.

Because it’s not that part that is steering the ship for the most part… it’s the unconscious.

This is why the pursuit of love can be such a heart wrenching, heartbreaking and exhausting struggle.

“Why does this keep happening to me?” we might ask, as somehow we end up yet again feeling the same pain, the same frustration, the same disappointment.

This is because our unconscious blueprint has not yet been resolved… and it is guiding our choices.

The people we are attracted to, the types of conflict and drama that we get into in relationships, the way we end relationships.

When I work with clients… we always end up working here.

One client, for her, early life was chaotic and unstable filled with drama.

Love was only felt at the peak of the instability… and so what happens when her relationship entered moments of calm and peace? She became very uncomfortable and started to look for the next thing to complain about, the next thing to find wrong, the next thing to turn into a drama.

Another client experienced several losses of important male figures in her life. Love is something she never really gets to keep. And so she is pulled over and over to the unavailable man, the one who wants her but doesn’t choose her. The one who won’t stay.

It’s all there… the pattern is clear, if you are willing to look at it.

It is a brave soul though who is willing to take that kind of self-responsibility.

To look at one’s life and say… “Hey what is it that I am doing to participate in this?”

Our culture isn’t really a fan of this type of accountability, it much prefers to blame the other with accusations of narcissist, too-muchness, selfishness, and so on… 

“How dare you suggest that it’s my fault - you are victim shaming!” the cry echoes throughout the halls of social media.

The problem with that perspective is that it DOES make us a victim of life… a victim of chance… a victim of others.

It says: “I hope something good will happen to me, but I have no power to create it for myself so I will simply take what is given, and if I don’t like it I will complain about it to anyone who will listen”

Taking responsibility is deeply humbling.

Because when we do… we have to ask, every time… “how did I participate in this happening?”

Because the reality always is, we did participate.

We chose to go on that first date, that second date, that third date, make love, move in together… or whatever else that happened…

Why? Why did we fall in love with *that* person?

That’s the question to ask.

The beautiful thing is, when we do finally ask ourselves what part we played in the creation of our own life experience, we have just taken the first step towards real power and real transformation.

We are moving towards becoming a conscious participant in the creation of our own reality.

Through the process of transmuting the unconscious into consciousness... as Carl Jung so famously said until we do that it will "rule our life and we will call it fate".

Summer Berry Meringue Cake 

Ingredients
CAKE
  Cooking spray
  2/3 cup unsalted butter (5 1/3 ounces), softened
  1 3/4 cups granulated sugar, divided
  4 large eggs, at room temperature
  1 3/4 cups cake flour (such as Swans Down) (about 6 5/8 ounces)
  2 teaspoons baking powder
  3/4 teaspoon kosher salt
  1/2 cup sour cream
  1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
  1/2 ounce freeze-dried strawberries (about 2/3 cup), coarsely crushed (about 1/3 cup)
  4 large egg whites, at room temperature
  1/4 teaspoon cream of tartar
TOPPING
  1/4 cup seedless raspberry jam
  1 pound fresh berries (such as blackberries, raspberries, and stemmed and quartered strawberries) or sliced stone fruit
  1 1/2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice
  4 1/4 teaspoons ground sumac, divided
  1/4 teaspoon kosher salt, divided
  1 cup heavy cream
  1/2 cup sour cream
  1/2 teaspoon vanilla extract
  1 tablespoon granulated sugar

Directions
Make the cake 
 1 Preheat oven to 350°F. Line a 13- x 9-inch baking pan with parchment paper, leaving a 2-inch overhang on both long sides; lightly grease with cooking spray. Beat butter and 3/4 cup sugar with a stand mixer fitted with paddle attachment on medium speed until light and fluffy, about 4 minutes. Add whole eggs, 1 at a time, beating well after each addition.

 2 Sift together cake flour, baking powder, and salt. Add flour mixture to butter mixture in 3 additions alternately with sour cream (2 additions of 1/4 cup each), beginning and ending with flour mixture, beating on low speed until just combined after each addition. Stir in vanilla. Fold in freeze-dried strawberries. Spread mixture in prepared pan, and set aside.

 3 Beat egg whites with stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium speed until foamy, about 30 seconds. Add cream of tartar. With mixer running on medium speed, gradually add remaining 1 cup sugar, 1 tablespoon at a time, beating until all sugar is incorporated and mixture is glossy and forms stiff peaks, about 5 minutes. Spread meringue in an even layer on top of cake batter, leaving a 1/2-inch border around edges of pan.

 4 Bake cake in preheated oven until meringue is dry and a wooden skewer inserted through meringue and cake comes out clean, 22 to 26 minutes. Let cake cool in pan 10 minutes. Using parchment as handles, carefully transfer cake to a wire rack. (Meringue will crack.) Let cool completely, about 1 hour.

Make the topping 
 1 Meanwhile, place raspberry jam in a medium-size microwavable bowl, and microwave on high until smooth and melted, 30 to 45 seconds, stirring every 15 seconds. Add berries, lemon juice, 4 teaspoons sumac, and 1/8 teaspoon salt; toss to coat. Let stand at room temperature at least 30 minutes or up to 1 hour, stirring occasionally.

 2 Combine heavy cream, sour cream, vanilla, and remaining 1/8 teaspoon salt in bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment. With mixer running on medium speed, gradually add sugar, beating until medium peaks form, 1 to 2 minutes.

 3 Transfer cake to a serving board, and remove parchment paper. Top with cream mixture. Just before serving, top with berry mixture. Sprinkle with remaining 1/4 teaspoon sumac.

Spice Apple Cake 

Ingredients
•1/2 stick butter, plus extra for loaf pan
•3 Granny Smith apples, peeled and cored, cut into 1/2-inch dice and tossed with a little lemon juice
•1/2 lemon, juiced
•1 cup apple cider
•1 3/4 cups all-purpose flour, plus extra for loaf pan
•1 teaspoon ground cinnamon
•1 teaspoon baking soda
•3 or 4 grates fresh nutmeg (about 1/2 teaspoon)
•3/4 cup brown sugar
•3/4 cup sugar
•Pinch kosher salt
•1 egg
•1 teaspoon vanilla extract
•1/2 cup toasted and chopped walnuts
•1/2 cup golden Raisins

Cream Cheese Icing:
•One 8-ounce package cream cheese, at room temperature
•1 stick butter, at room temperature
•1 cup powdered sugar
•1 teaspoon vanilla extract
•1/2 lemon, juiced

Directions
  Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F.
  Melt the butter in a large saute pan over medium heat. Toss in the apples and stir to coat them with the butter. Add the lemon juice and the apple cider. Cook until the apples have softened and the cider has reduced by half. Transfer the mixture to a food processor and pulse into a coarse paste. Reserve.
  In a large mixing bowl combine the flour, cinnamon, baking soda, nutmeg, both of the sugars and a pinch of salt. Make a well in the dry ingredients and add the pureed apples, the egg and vanilla. Stir to combine. Toss in the walnuts and raisins.
  Butter & flour a loaf pan. Pour batter into the prepared pan & put in preheated oven. Bake until a toothpick, inserted in the center comes out clean, about 40 to 45 minutes.
  Remove the pan from the oven and let cool for 10 minutes. Remove cake from pan & cool completely.
  Cut cake in half equatorially & spread half of the icing on the bottom layer. Replace the top half & ice top of the cake, leave the sides bare. Slice & serve.
Cream Cheese Icing:
  Beat together all of the ingredients with a mixer until light & fluffy.

Baked Shells with Gremolata Breadcrumbs

Ingredients
  1 tablespoon plus 1 3/4 teaspoon kosher salt, divided  
  1 (16-ounce) package medium pasta shells 
  3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil, divided 
  ¼ cup unsalted butter 
  1/3 cup all-purpose flour (about 1 1/2 ounces) 
  3 1/2 cups half-and-half, warmed
  1/2 cup whole milk, warmed 
  8 ounces Fontina cheese, shredded (about 2 cups), divided 
  8 ounces sharp cheddar cheese, shredded (about 2 cups), divided 
  1 ¼ teaspoons onion powder
  1 ¼ teaspoons garlic powder
  1 ¼ teaspoons ground white pepper 
  ¼ teaspoon ground nutmeg
  1/2 teaspoon black pepper 
  1/2 cup panko breadcrumbs
  1/2 cup finely chopped fresh flat-leaf parsley
  6 (2- x  1/2-inch) lemon peel strips, minced (about 2 teaspoons) 
  1 small garlic clove, grated  

Directions
 1 Preheat oven to 350°F with rack 10 inches from heat. Bring a large saucepan of water to a boil over high. Add 1 tablespoon salt and stir in shells; cook according to package directions for al dente. Drain shells and transfer to a large bowl. Add 1 tablespoon oil; toss to coat. Set cooked shells aside.

 2 Wipe saucepan clean. Add butter and melt over medium. Whisk in flour; cook, whisking constantly, until mixture is lightly browned, 3 to 4 minutes. Gradually whisk in half-and-half and milk until sauce is smooth. Bring just to a simmer over medium-high, whisking occasionally. Reduce heat to low; simmer, whisking often, until no floury taste remains, about 5 minutes. Remove from heat. Gradually whisk in 1 1/2 cups Fontina and 1 1/2 cups cheddar until smooth. Whisk in onion powder, garlic powder, white pepper, and nutmeg. Fold in cooked shells. Season with 1 1/2 teaspoons salt and the black pepper. Spread mixture evenly in a 2-quart broiler-safe baking dish. Sprinkle with remaining 1/2 cup Fontina and remaining 1/2 cup cheddar.

 3 Bake in preheated oven until bubbling around edges, about 20 minutes. Increase oven temperature to broil. (Do not remove baking dish from oven.) Broil until browned in spots, 3 to 4 minutes. Remove from oven; let cool 5 minutes.

 4 Meanwhile, heat remaining 2 tablespoons oil in a medium skillet over medium. Add panko; cook, stirring constantly, until deep golden, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a medium bowl and let cool 2 minutes. Stir in parsley, lemon peel, and garlic. Season with remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Serve gremolata breadcrumbs with shells.

Strawberry Cheesecake Overnight Oats 

Ingredients
  1/2 cup graham cracker crumbs
  1 cup plain Greek-style yogurt, 2% milkfat
  1 cup whole milk
  1 teaspoon vanilla extract
  1 teaspoon lemon juice
  1 tablespoon honey
  6 strawberries, chopped, plus more as needed to garnish
  1 tablespoon chia seeds
  1 cup rolled oats (see Notes from the Food & Wine Test Kitchen)
  1/2 cup sliced almonds

Directions
 1 Divide graham cracker crumbs between 2 Mason jars, and press down with a spoon to form a crust at bottom of each jar. Whisk together yogurt, milk, vanilla, lemon juice, and honey in a bowl until fully blended. Stir in strawberries, chia seeds, and oats. Transfer mixture to jars, cover jars with lids, and refrigerate 8 hours or overnight before eating; oats can be refrigerated up to 48 hours before serving. Garnish each jar with strawberries and sliced almonds and serve.

Charred Cabbage with Coconut, Garlic, and Chili Crisp

Ingredients
  15 medium garlic cloves, peeled
  1/2 cup canola oil
  2 tablespoons  finely grated palm sugar or granulated sugar
  2 tablespoons Thai fish sauce (such as Megachef)
  1/2 teaspoon black pepper
  1 (2 1/4-pound) head green cabbage, trimmed of outer leaves and cut through core into 8 wedges
  1/4 cup coconut milk or mayonnaise
  3/4 teaspoon kosher salt
  1/2 cup chili crisp (such as Fly By Jing)

Directions
 1 Cook garlic and oil in a small saucepan over low, swirling occasionally, until garlic is golden and semi-softened, about 12 minutes. Drain garlic-infused oil into a small bowl. Transfer garlic cloves to a second small bowl. Mash cloves using a fork or spoon; stir in palm sugar, fish sauce, and black pepper. Set aside garlic chutney and reserved oil.

 2 While garlic cooks, set a steamer rack inside a large pot filled with 1 inch of water; bring to a boil over high. Place cabbage on steamer rack; cover with lid, and cook until bright green and tender, about 5 minutes. Remove cabbage; pat dry.


 3 Preheat a large cast-iron skillet over high for 5 minutes. Whisk together coconut milk and 1/4 cup reserved garlic oil in a small bowl. Brush cut sides of each cabbage wedge with 1 tablespoon coconut milk mixture; sprinkle wedges evenly with salt. Working in 2 batches, cook cabbage wedges in skillet until charred, 2 minutes per side.


 4 To serve, spread 1 1/2 teaspoons reserved garlic chutney over charred sides of each cabbage wedge; drizzle each wedge with 2 tablespoons chili crisp.

16 million 384 thousand citizens of Iran voted for Masoud Pezeshkian

Earlier, the first round of elections did not determine the winner because none of the candidates won more than 50 per cent of the votes.

According to Reuters, many voters are sceptical about Pezeshkian's ability to fulfil his campaign promises, as he has publicly stated that he has no intention of confronting Iran's ruling elite.

The enigmatic Aqueduct of Piedra de Cumbemayo, Cajamarca, Peru. 

It is the prodigy of pre-Hispanic Andean hydraulic engineering. Its sophisticated design makes it possible for the waters to "rise" and pass from one basin to another. Andean engineers mastered the knowledge and applications of gravity, 2000 years before it was known in Europe and was formulated by Isaac Newton in his book Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published on July 5, 1687.

Due to its complex and well-elaborated aqueduct system, it is not surprising that the name Cumbemayo derives from the Quechua term kumpi Mayu, which means, "Canal well done" or Humpi Mayu, which means "Narrow River". Coming to be considered one of the most notable hydraulic works in Pre-Columbian America. 

The archaeological complex of Cumbemayo was built by the Pre-Inca culture, Cajamarca.
Dr. Julio C. Tello was the first person to study this place in 1937. Archaeologist who came to be impressed by its well-elaborated system of channels, in addition to the petroglyphs that adorn this complex, and that to this day still do not have been deciphered. 

According to Tello, this canal was possibly built in 1000 BC. Later investigations indicated that the aqueduct was used for many centuries, and they even point to the worship found on the edge of the friars, very close to the place.
The aqueduct is located at about 3,600 meters above sea level. The channels reach a maximum depth of 50 cm. And wide about 30 cm. 

In addition, zigzag elbows and right angles were used in order to reduce the speed of the waters; and, at the same time, avoid soil erosion. Even today it is possible to see water running through its channels. The approximate total length of this aqueduct is 850 m.

🟣 The best time for sowing is spring-summer. When seedlings appear, open the glass and be sure to lengthen the daylight hours to 12 hours, using a fluorescent lamp. The pomegranate blooms very beautifully.

🟣 Care features are regular (but not excessive!) watering and rest for a couple of months - November-December. Representative_Docs: A rifle with a magazine larger than 3 bullets.
With a rifle you can brace it into your shoulder, longer barrel. Pistol what are you bracing? A shorter barrel. A pistol is much harder to shoot than a rifle.

Because it is a low diameter bullet, the effective area for the cartridge pressure to bear on the rear of the projectile is lower and so the effective force is less. Thus in order to get adequate velocity, the force needs to be applied for longer. This is why AR-15s really benefit from a longer barrel. A 20” barrel produces significantly more velocity than a 16” which produces even more significant velocity than a 12”. A handgun length (3-5”) barrel in 5.56 is almost no better than .22 long rifle and is incredible loud. So thats why handguns use fat diameter bullets - more force more acceleration in a short barrel is worth the bad ballistic properties. Another thing is that handguns are small light and should recoil less. They need to operate at lower pressures. 5.56 operates at 62,500 psi, and 9mm acp at 35,000 psi. So 9mm barrels and locking assemblies can afford to be much weaker. Getting back to the loudness thing - in a short fat barrel the pressure reduces quickly as the bullet moves down the barrel because the volume increases rapidly and the pressure reduces rapidly. With 5.56 the volume increases slowly so the pressure stays high longer. Thus a long barrel for 9mm makes far less velocity improvements than for 5.56. Plus, the pressure of the gas exposed to the atmosphere when the bullet leaves is lower for 9mm from a short barrel than 5.56. So this means less noise and wasted powder potential energy. Ive shot short barrel 5.56 and the sound is shocking. That is broadly why handguns chose the inferior ballistics of large slow moving bullet over a small fast one. The benefits of the latter do not outweigh the drawbacks for the purpose of a handgun, and the opposite is true for rifles.
